newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian electricity instruments said successful.
newsitem.headline: Australian electricity instruments said successful.

text.p: Over-the-counter electricity trading instruments had become "tearaway" products in Australia's eastern states since the opening of the National Electricity Market (NEM1), a Gas and Electricity Risk Management Conference here heard on Wednesday.
This was why the Sydney Futures Exchange would launch trading in electricity futures contracts in September, Sandy Wilkinson, head of energy at merchant bank RMB Australia, said.
Electricity price volatility in the east-coast states of Victoria and New South Wales (NSW), now linked by NEM1, was of key importance for futures and hedging instruments, he said.
While price volatility in Victoria early this year stabilised in May and July, with the establishment of open market trading, volatility had recently returned, he said.
OTC contract forms now ran the gamut of swaps, vesting contracts, options, trading on price periods and inter-regional swaps, he said.

Wilkinson, who described the Australian market as still immature, said that trades in electricity market products were conducted between all players in the industry, including retailers, generators and institutional investment houses. Institutions were led by Macquarie Bank Ltd and Societe
Generale, while swaps were conducted through the International Swaps Dealers Association (ISDA).
The Australian Financial Markets Association was also producing a guide to OTC electricity implement dealing, he said.
"We're all on the phone to each other every day," Wilkinson told Reuters, commenting on how the market worked.
Screen-traded futures contracts would be a new tool but would not displace OTC products entirely, Wilkinson predicted.

Futures would add a new averaging technique and an ability to enter and exit positions. They would also provide good price discovery and aid convergence between physical and financial markets, he said.

A series of transitions had so far characterised electricity contract trading in Australia, especially with the establishment of NEM1 on May 4 this year and the removal of the "throttle" physical restraint of 800 MW on trading on July 1.
Changes in hedge trading had accompanied the entry of market players and the evolution of traded electricity itself, he said.
The market so far had featured retailers hedging to win customers and generators selling hedges to protect market share.
Electricity swaps included one party paying a fixed price and the other party paying a floating or pool price for a fixed or variable volume, he said.
An ISDA swap contract could be for either a single half-hour of electricity or for many years of half-hours, he said.

Wilkinson described vesting contracts, which involve franchised customer supplies, as a form of government OTC swap. They could be expected to wind down when franchising ends in NSW on June 30, 2000, he said.

Traded electricity options involve the usual range of specifications including puts and calls, usually with payment of a premium. Other types of contracts are based on average price periods, trading intervals, peak periods, shoulder periods, offpeak periods and combinations, he said.
Swaps may also be effected on an inter-regional basis.
"What's your appetitte, how big's your pocket?" Wilkinson asked in reference to inter-regional trading possibilities.

Wilkinson said electricity demand was fundamentally driven by temperatures in central business districts, the type of day and time of week, while price spikes were governed by transmission and unplanned generator outages.
